scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Veeragase originates from the Hindu mythological traditions of Karnataka, specifically tied to the Veerashaiva/Lingayat faith.
It centers on the story of Veerabhadra, the warrior deity born from a lock of Shiva's hair following the death of Sati at the Daksha Yajna.
Historically, the dance has been the exclusive preserve of the Jangama or Maheshwara clan.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Veeragase is performed during significant Hindu festivals and Veerashaiva religious ceremonies.
It is a ritualistic reenactment of divine justice and fury, intended to honor Shiva and Veerabhadra.
The act of mouth-piercing signifies deep devotion and the suppression of the ego.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by intense, energy-sapping movements performed in groups of two, four, or six.
Dancers maintain a high level of vigor throughout the performance, often involving wide stances and rhythmic stepping that synchronizes with the percussion.
A lead singer provides the narrative structure while dancers embody the warrior spirit.
Watch for Shastra Dharane.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical accompaniment is loud and percussive, dominated by the sambal and dimmu drums.
Cymbals provide sharp rhythmic accents, while the shehnai adds a melodic layer.
Listen for the Sambal, Dimmu, Cymbals, Shehnai.

The sound is dominated by the thunderous, heavy beats of the sambal and dimmu drums, punctuated by the sharp metallic clash of cymbals. A lead singer chants the epic of Daksha Yajna in a powerful, narrative style, often accompanied by the high-pitched, wailing melody of the shehnai.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear traditional warrior-like attire, often including elaborate headgear and ornaments.
A key ritualistic element involves the piercing of a needle through the mouth.
The performance often takes place in temple courtyards or during religious processions, centered around the Nandikolu pole.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The performers are collectively known as Lingadevaru or Maheshwaras, belonging to the Jangama clan; specific individual historical names are not provided in the sources.
While prevalent across Karnataka, it is also known by the name Guggla in certain contexts or regions.
The dance is passed down through the Jangama (Maheshwara) clan of the Veerashaiva/Lingayat community.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Veeragase is a sacred ritual of the Veerashaiva/Lingayat community and must only be performed by members of the Jangama (Maheshwara) clan. It involves ritualistic mouth piercing; observers should maintain respect for the religious sanctity of the act.
